title: A clinical comparison of two different fabrication methods with regard to the accuracy of all-ceramic restorations. A prospective, randomized controlled clinical trial.
summary:
Over the course of a lifetime, teeth undergo wear and tear. In cases of advanced wear, restoration is necessary not only for aesthetic reasons but especially for functional reasons to ensure the health of the temporomandibular joints. This applies equally to cases of congenital insufficient development of tooth structure or excessive wear of tooth structure caused by acidic beverages, as well as by severe grinding and clenching. The replacement of lost tooth structure or the lengthening of teeth has already been performed for you using non-invasive, printed restorations as long-term temporaries. You have worn these restorations for a period of three years. Adaptation to the new bite situation has now been completed without any complaints. It is now necessary to replace the long-term temporary restorations with definitive, all-ceramic restorations. 
All-ceramic materials have been established in restorative dentistry for years. The material used is a zirconia ceramic (IPS e-max ZirCAD) from Ivoclar. This ceramic allows us to fabricate all restoration geometries for single-tooth restorations, as well as bridge restorations or implant restorations. 
To ensure proper cleaning of the teeth and the margins of the restorations, we would like to perform a minimally invasive preparation of the teeth. This means that the existing long-term temporary restorations will remain partially in place on the teeth as build-up material. The teeth must be ground down at the margins so that the restoration margins end in healthy tooth structure. Furthermore, the teeth must be shortened on the occlusal surface or incisal edge to ensure sufficient space for the all-ceramic restoration. All restorations will be defect-oriented and designed to be as minimally invasive as possible. 
The aim of this clinical study is to collect and evaluate long-term data on all-ceramic restorations. The parameters to be examined include material and tooth wear, color stability, and your personal satisfaction before and after treatment, which will be assessed via questionnaires. Furthermore, we aim to compare analog and digital treatment approaches. Furthermore, the clinical impact on the complex movements of the lower jaw and temporomandibular joints following the placement of restorations has not yet been digitally measured and evaluated.
conditions: Evaluation of two different fabrication methods for the production of all-ceramic restorations
